title: PostgreSQL in depth
subtitle: Learn how Postgres stores, cleans, indexes and copies your rows, so it does not stop taking writes on a Monday morning.

c.v: At 05:35 UTC on 4 February 2019, one database stopped taking writes at Mandrill, Mailchimp's email service for apps. The database was a Postgres
called shard4. It went into "safety shutdown mode".
must clean up old IDs in time. On shard4 it had fallen behind or failed, and the IDs hit their limit.
The team had seen it coming. In November 2018 they found the IDs at about half their limit during peak load. They added a ticket to set up more monitoring.
The fix was slow. Vacuuming the whole shard was estimated to take up to 40 days. Two tables were terabytes in size. Mandrill deletes queued mail after 48 hours, so time mattered.
At 19:12 UTC on 5 February, the team truncated those large tables. The vacuum finished about an hour later. Service came back after about 40 hours. By 22:40 they had alerts for wraparound.
Sentry had the same outage in 2015. It too ended by truncating one large table.
Postgres does not change a row in place. An

So every busy table creates garbage all the time. An old version that no transaction can see is a

VACUUM has a second job that people forget. It marks old rows as "frozen", so their transaction IDs can be reused safely.
Skip the first job and you get bloat. Skip the second and Postgres stops writes.
In Postgres, every update and delete leaves work for VACUUM. Your job is to keep autovacuum fast enough, and to make sure nothing stops it.
Step through one update, from new row version to cleanup.
Autovacuum and when it falls behind
Autovacuum vacuums a table after enough rows have changed. By default the trigger is 50 rows plus 20% of the table.
On a table with 100 million rows, that means about 20 million dead tuples before it starts. By default, 3 workers share the whole server.
When it falls behind, dead tuples pile up and the table bloats. Scans read more pages. A long open transaction or a forgotten
Transaction IDs (XIDs) are 32 bits. Postgres compares them in a circle: for each ID, two billion are "older" and two billion are "newer".
An unfrozen row older than that would suddenly look like it is from the future.
So every table must be vacuumed at least once every two billion transactions.

q.v: UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = 7
. What happens to the old row in Postgres?

options.v: It is changed in place on disk.
It stays as an old row version until no transaction can see it, and VACUUM frees its space.
It is moved to an undo log at once.

why.v: Postgres writes a new row version and keeps the old one for older snapshots. VACUUM removes it later.

q.v: A database logs "must be vacuumed within 39985967 transactions". What does that mean?

options.v: Autovacuum is keeping up. Nothing to do.
Old transaction IDs are near the wraparound limit. Find what blocks VACUUM and fix it now.
You must restart Postgres in single-user mode at once.

why.v: In PostgreSQL 18 and earlier, the warning starts 40 million transactions before wraparound (100 million from version 19). Below 3 million, Postgres refuses new writes. The docs say single-user mode is usually not needed.

q.v: Which update is most likely to be a HOT update?

options.v: Changing a non-indexed counter when the page has free space.
Any update on a table with a GIN index.

why.v: HOT needs no change to indexed columns and room on the same page.

q.v: You want to move to a new major Postgres version with little downtime. Which tool fits?

options.v: Physical streaming replication to a standby on the new version.
Logical replication to a server on the new version.

why.v: Physical streaming does not work across major versions. Logical replication does, but it does not copy schema changes, and before version 19 it does not copy sequence values.

q.v: Why can 2,000 direct connections hurt a Postgres server even when most are idle?

options.v: Each connection is its own backend process, and Postgres sizes shared memory by max_connections.
Postgres has a hard limit of 100 connections.

why.v: Postgres starts one process per connection. The default limit is about 100, and raising it costs memory.
